title: See and Be Seen
summary: Riders should scan 10 to 15 seconds ahead along their path of travel.
Drivers involved in motorcycle crashes often say they did not see the rider; a motorcycle's small size also makes it seem farther away and slower than it really is.

Most motorcycle crashes happen in daylight, so dress to be seen: bright orange, red, yellow or green jackets or vests and reflective tape on your helmet and gear help; if you won't wear bright colors, consider a reflective vest.

Keeping the headlight on at all times is the best way to be noticed; research shows a daytime headlight makes a motorcycle twice as noticeable to oncoming drivers, and the manual suggests riders consider using high beam in daylight for extra visibility.
A motorcycle brake light is usually less noticeable than a car's, so flash it before slowing or stopping, especially when being tailgated.

Know the hand signals and routinely use them along with your electronic signals; the manual's drawing shows an arm held straight out for a left turn, a forearm bent upward for a right turn, and an arm angled downward to slow or stop.

Turn signals tell others your intentions and make you more visible (a driver behind you is more likely to notice a turn signal than a taillight); use them for every lane change even when no one seems to be around, and always cancel them afterward.

Be prepared to use the horn in an emergency or when a vehicle entering your lane may not leave you room to get by safely; be ready to stop or swerve if a driver in the next lane is closing fast on another vehicle and may try to pass, a parked car's door opens, or a pedestrian or bicyclist is in the street.
Each lane offers three paths of travel; choose a position that keeps you out of blind spots and visible in the mirrors of vehicles ahead, and pass through blind spots quickly.
SPIDER stands for Scan, Predict, Identify, Decide, Execute, Rely.
In city riding, look between half a block and a full block ahead; on the highway, look as far ahead as you can while keeping control, and watch curves and ramps for oil and gravel.

Check mirrors every few seconds, and closely when slowing or stopping (if a vehicle following you is dangerously close, it can be safer to keep going than to stop); turn your head to look before changing lanes; convex mirrors make vehicles behind seem farther away than they are; and intersections, meaning anywhere traffic can cross your path, are the greatest danger.

questions.q: How far ahead along your path of travel should you scan?
options: 2 to 4 seconds
5 to 8 seconds
10 to 15 seconds
20 to 30 seconds
questions.explanation: The manual lists scanning 10 to 15 seconds ahead as one of the ways to reduce your chance of a crash.

questions.q: In crashes involving motorcycles, what do other drivers often cite as the leading cause?
options: They did not see the rider
The rider was speeding
Poor road conditions
Mechanical failure of the motorcycle
questions.explanation: Drivers frequently say a lack of rider visibility was the main cause of the crash.

questions.q: Because of a motorcycle's small size, other drivers may misjudge it. How?
options: It seems closer and faster than it is
It seems farther away and slower than it is
It seems closer but slower than it is
It seems farther away but faster than it is
questions.explanation: Smaller vehicles appear more distant and slower-moving than they really are, so drivers can misjudge a rider's distance and speed.

questions.q: When do most accidents involving motorcycles happen?
options: At night
At dawn and dusk
During rain or fog
During daylight hours
questions.explanation: The manual states that most motorcycle crashes occur in daylight, which is why bright clothing matters even during the day.

questions.q: If you choose not to wear brightly colored clothing, what does the manual suggest?
options: Ride only on roads with light traffic
Wear a reflective vest
Keep your hazard flashers on
Ride only at night
questions.explanation: A reflective vest is recommended as a way to alert drivers to your presence when you are not wearing bright colors.

questions.q: What is the best way to alert other drivers to your presence on a motorcycle?
options: Sound your horn often
Ride close behind the vehicle ahead
Keep your headlight on at all times
Rev your engine at intersections
questions.explanation: Keeping the headlight on at all times is described as the best way to make drivers aware of you.

questions.q: According to research cited in the manual, how much more noticeable to oncoming drivers is a motorcycle with its headlight on during daylight?
options: About 10 percent more
About 50 percent more
Three times as noticeable
Twice as noticeable
questions.explanation: Research shows a daytime headlight makes a motorcycle twice as noticeable to oncoming drivers.

questions.q: When is it especially important to flash your brake light before slowing?
options: When no other vehicles are behind you
When you are being followed too closely
When you are wearing brightly colored gear
When you are riding below the speed limit
questions.explanation: A tailgater may be focused only on your motorcycle and unaware of hazards ahead, so flashing the brake light warns them you are slowing.

questions.q: Which hand signal indicates a left turn?
options: Arm held straight out to the side
Arm out to the side, forearm bent up
Arm out to the side, angled downward
Arm raised straight up over the head
questions.explanation: In the manual's drawing, a left turn is an arm held straight out to the side. A forearm bent upward means a right turn, and an arm angled downward means slow or stop.

questions.q: Should you use your turn signal when changing lanes if no other vehicles seem to be around?
options: No, signals are only needed when vehicles are nearby
Only on highways
Only at night
Yes, always signal lane changes
questions.explanation: The manual recommends always signaling a lane change, even when no vehicle may be present.

questions.q: Why is a turn signal that is left blinking dangerous?
options: It makes your motorcycle harder for drivers to see
It may lead a driver to pull into your path
It tells other drivers you are about to speed up
It hides your brake light from drivers behind you
questions.explanation: An uncanceled signal can lead a driver to expect your turn and move into your path, so check your instrument panel after turning.

questions.q: A driver in the next lane is closing fast on another vehicle and may cut into your lane. Besides being ready to use your horn, what should you be prepared to do?
options: Speed up to block the driver
Pull alongside the driver and stay there
Be ready to stop or swerve
Move closer to the vehicle ahead
questions.explanation: The manual's horn section names this as one of the situations where you should be prepared to stop or swerve away from danger, since the driver may cut into your lane.

questions.q: How many distinct paths of travel does each marked traffic lane give a motorcycle rider?
options: One
Two
Four
Three
questions.explanation: Each marked lane offers a rider three paths of travel for choosing a visible position.

questions.q: In the SPIDER process, what does the "D" stand for?
options: Detect
Drive
Decide
Defend
questions.explanation: SPIDER stands for Scan, Predict, Identify, Decide, Execute, and Rely.

questions.q: When riding in the city, how far ahead should you look?
options: One-half to one full block
Just the vehicle directly ahead
Two to three blocks
As far as the next traffic light only
questions.explanation: In city traffic, the manual advises keeping your eyes between half a block and a full block ahead.

questions.q: Where should you pay particular attention for oil and gravel on the road surface?
options: On long straightaways
On curves and ramps
On steep uphill grades
On roads with low speed limits
questions.explanation: Curves and ramps are singled out as places where oil and gravel tend to collect.

questions.q: How do convex motorcycle mirrors affect what you see behind you?
options: Objects look closer than they are
Objects look larger than they are
They have no effect on apparent distance
Objects look farther away than they are
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors show more of the road behind but make vehicles appear more distant, so practice judging distance with them.

questions.q: Before changing lanes, what should a responsible rider do in addition to checking mirrors?
options: Turn the head to check for vehicles
Sound the horn before moving over
Flash the high beam at the car ahead
Turn on the hazard flashers briefly
questions.explanation: Before changing lanes, the manual says to turn your head and look for any vehicle coming up behind you or trying to pass, rather than relying on mirrors alone.

questions.q: According to the manual, which location poses the greatest danger to a motorcycle rider?
options: Tunnels
Open highways
Intersections
Bridges
questions.explanation: Intersections, meaning any place traffic may cross your path, are described as the greatest danger.

questions.q: You are riding behind another vehicle. Where should you position your motorcycle?
options: Where the driver can see you in the vehicle's mirrors
Close behind the vehicle, where it blocks the wind
On the lane line, so you can slip past slow traffic
Off a rear corner, in the driver's blind spot
questions.explanation: Pick a spot in your lane where the driver in front can see you in their mirrors, not one of their blind spots, and use your lights along with your lane position to help others notice you.

questions.q: Compared with a car's brake lights, how noticeable is a motorcycle's brake light, according to the manual?
options: Usually more noticeable, because it sits higher
About as noticeable, since both must meet the same standards
Usually less noticeable, especially when the taillight is on
More noticeable at night, but less noticeable by day
questions.explanation: Motorcycle brake lights are usually harder to notice than a car's, particularly with the taillight on, so flash yours before you slow or stop.

questions.q: What does the manual say about how well a driver behind you can see your turn signal?
options: They are less likely to see it than your taillight
They are more likely to see it than your taillight
They can see it only if your headlight is on
They can't see it in daylight, so use hand signals instead
questions.explanation: Besides showing your intentions, turn signals make you more visible: a driver behind you is more likely to notice a turn signal than a taillight.

questions.q: How often does the manual recommend checking your mirrors while riding?
options: Every few seconds
About once a minute
Only before changing lanes
Only when slowing or stopping
questions.explanation: Checking your mirrors every few seconds lets you respond safely when traffic conflicts or hazards come up. Check them with extra care whenever you slow down or make a sudden stop.
